extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science and scientific method; scientifically-literate readers interested in epistemology and the foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for when to believe, suspend judgment about, or disbelieve empirical and mathematical claims; includes the nature of mathematical/geomterical premises, limits of applying mathematics to other sciences, and standards for assessing extraordinary claims (e.g., miracles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of numbers by modes of formation
rubrics_metrics.description: A number name (two, three, etc.) connotes how single objects of a particular kind must be combined to form that aggregate (modes of formation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every arithmetical proposition is a statement about one of the modes of formation of a given number; knowing one mode for each number permits deductive determination of all other modes. Select a uniform, simple mode of formation for names of numbers to aid comprehension and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive warrant underlying arithmetic ('sums of equals are equals')
rubrics_metrics.description: The general law 'The sums of equals are equals' (or 'Whatever is made up of parts is made up of the parts of those parts') is the inductive truth that warrants arithmetic operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highest-order inductive law, evident to the senses across phenomena that can be numbered, is the basis for believing arithmetic results (e.g., 5 + 2 = 7). Arithmetical demonstrations apply it or truths deducible from it at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic notation as a tool for general reasoning about functions
rubrics_metrics.description: To reason generally about functions of numbers we require notation (algebra) that can denote arbitrary numbers and their modes of formation from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbols (a, b, n, (a+b)^n, etc.) to express general problems — e.g., determine what a function F will be of any function of a number — allowing the derivation of theorems (e.g., the binomial theorem) that assert identities between different modes of formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical axioms and definitions as premises of geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry rests on a few general principles: (1) sums of equals are equal, (2) things equal to the same thing are equal to one another, and (3) magnitudes that can be applied to coincide are equal; plus definitions asserting existence of objects (straight lines, angles, circles, etc.) with one essential property each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms and minimal definitions serve as ultimate premises from which theorems are deduced. Choose one characteristic property for each geometrical kind as the basis for reasoning; no more is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles enabling deductive measurement in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain spatial laws make geometry highly deductive: (a) magnitudes of enclosed spaces are determined by their bounding lines and angles; (b) length of a line (given other things) is measured by the angle it subtends and vice versa; (c) angle at an inaccessible point is measured by angles with a chosen third line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these relations, measurement of many magnitudes can be reduced to measuring a single straight line and a number of angles (as in triangulation and trigonometrical surveys), enabling far-reaching deductions from few data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on applicability of mathematical principles to other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods are inapplicable where (a) causes are imperfectly accessible to observation so numerical laws cannot be induced, (b) causes are extremely numerous and intermixed so computation of aggregate effects is infeasible, or (c) causes are in perpetual fluctuation (e.g., physiology, social science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical accuracy often comes 'at the expense of the reality of the inquiry' when phenomena are complex; apply mathematical models only where causes can be sufficiently isolated, observed, and rendered numerically tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disbelief (positive rejection vs absence of belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelief is not mere absence of belief; it is being fully persuaded that an opinion is false so that, even given apparently strong evidence, one would judge the witnesses or perceivers to be mistaken or deceitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between withholding belief (insufficient evidence) and actively disbelieving (evidence, when weighed against better inductions, supports the negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between improbability and impossibility in assessing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alleged fact contradicts approximate generalizations (not exhaustive inductions), it is 'improbable' and should be provisionally disbelieved according to a probability comparison; if it contradicts a completed induction grounded on rigorous evidence, it is 'impossible' and to be utterly disbelieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the strength/order of the inductive generalizations supporting the affirmative and the negative. Provisional refusal follows when the negative rests on stronger approximate generalizations; total rejection follows when a fact contradicts a law established by a complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for overturning an established law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged fact that contradicts a law of nature established by complete induction must be supported by evidence equivalent in strength to that by which the law was established to be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not accept apparent violations of a well-established causal law unless the evidence suffices to show a flaw in the induction that produced the law — i.e., the rejecting evidence must be at least as strong as the evidence that established the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to judge claims that seem to contradict causal laws (role of counteracting causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions to a causal law are only genuine contradictions if the asserted absence of the effect occurred without any adequate counteracting cause; otherwise the event may be the result of an intervening or counteracting cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate the probability that a known or unknown counteracting cause existed at the relevant time and place using knowledge of frequencies/rarities. If the presence of such a cause is more probable than the falsity of the testimony, accept the testimony; otherwise disbelieve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles considered as introduction of a new cause, not contradiction of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction of the law of cause and effect but is alleged to be a new effect produced by the introduction of a new cause (divine interposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a miracle invokes an additional cause, its credibility hinges on the antecedent probability that such a cause existed in the instance; extraordinary evidence is required to accept that a new cause operated, especially given general presumption in favor of the uniform government of nature by laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of miracle-credibility on prior belief in supernatural agency
rubrics_metrics.description: If one does not already believe in beings with supernatural power, no amount of evidence of an extraordinary event can, on its own, prove the existence of supernatural agency; those who already believe in such beings may weigh supernatural vs unknown natural explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which hypothesis (unknown natural cause vs supernatural agency) is more probable in the particular case, taking into account the supposed character of the supernatural agent and the conformity of the event to that character; otherwise prefer the unknown-natural-cause hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of approximate generalizations when weighing conflicting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When affirmative evidence rests on approximate generalizations, and the negative side also rests on approximate generalizations, determine which set of approximate generalizations is of higher order and thus more probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief or disbelief should be proportional to the preponderance of approximate generalizations until further investigation clarifies the matter; stronger pre-existing approximate generalizations favor disbelief of the novel claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing conflicts with uniformities of co-existence (properties of kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged facts that conflict with observed uniformities of co-existence (properties of kinds) — e.g., traveler tales of men with tails — should be judged against the established regularities of those kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with causal laws, determine whether the asserted exception is more plausibly explained by error, misperception, or fabrication, or by the presence of previously unknown instances; ordinary sense and prior uniformities generally warrant disbelief of extraordinary categorical claims until confirmed.
